The first day on the ward
It's Monday, Mara's first working day at the hospital. Her colleague Jonas, from Hamburg, shows her the ward. Then Dr Ayşe Yılmaz appears.
Hi, you're Mara, right? I'm Jonas. I work here too, on ward 4.
Hi, Jonas! Sorry, I don't speak German that well yet.
Oh yes you do, you speak very well! Where are you from?
From Romania. I've been learning German for two years. Do you speak Romanian?
No, unfortunately! I speak English and a little Spanish. Come on, here's the nurses' room.
How many patients do you have?
Today we have eighteen patients. And this is Dr Yılmaz.
Good morning! Are you Ms Ionescu, the new colleague? Welcome!
Good morning, Doctor! Thank you! Sorry, pardon? More slowly, please.
No problem! I speak Turkish at home too. You learn German every day.
And now, first of all, we have a coffee. That's how it's done here!
At the start of a word, “sp” is read “shp” and “st” is read “sht”: sprechen = “SHPREH-khen”, Station = “shtah-TSYOHN”.
“-tion” is read “-tsyohn”, stressed at the end: Station, Information.
1. The present tense of regular verbs
Take the infinitive (which ends in -en), cut off “-en” and add the endings. Example: wohnen → wohn- :
The wir / sie / Sie forms are identical to the infinitive. Easy to remember!
If the stem ends in -t or -d, an -e- is added to make it easier to pronounce: arbeiten → du arbeitest, er arbeitet; finden → er findet.
2. Verbs with a vowel change: sprechen

You'll learn them one at a time. Dictionaries mark them: “sprechen (spricht)”.
3. The golden rule: the verb in position 2

In a German statement, the conjugated verb is ALWAYS in second position. Position 1 can be the subject, but also an expression of time or place. If position 1 is taken by something else, the subject moves AFTER the verb:
“Heute ich arbeite” is wrong! If you start with “Heute”, the verb comes right after it: “Heute arbeite ich.”
In yes / no questions, the verb moves to position 1. In questions with a question word (wo, wie, was), the question word is in position 1 and the verb is still in position 2:
Language names are written with a capital letter (as in English) and usually end in -isch: Rumänisch, Englisch, Spanisch, Türkisch, Italienisch, Französisch. Exception: Deutsch.
I've been learning German for two years.
“man” = one / you / people (general subject), with the verb in the third person: “Das macht man so.” = That's how it's done.
Germans really appreciate it when someone tries to speak German. Don't be afraid to ask for something to be repeated!
Verb in position 2, subject after it.
